findings.title: Remove unverified remote script piped to shell in image build
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes mutable code from https://example.com/install.sh as root at build time with no version pin, checksum, or signature verification. Compromise or any later change to that script persists in the final image layers and can tamper with installed tools or the runtime environment. The pipe also masks curl failures: without --fail or pipefail, a failed download can produce empty input and a successful sh exit, silently producing an incomplete image, while HTTP error bodies are fed to the shell.

findings.title: Remove unpinned remote script piped to root shell
findings.whyItBreaks: The image build downloads mutable content from https://example.com/install.sh and executes it as root with sh, with no pinned version, checksum, or signature verification and with -L following redirects. Anyone able to alter that URL, its redirects, or its hosting gains arbitrary code execution in the build and can persist backdoored binaries, secrets theft, or poisoned layers into every produced image. The added curl invocation also lacks --fail, so HTTP errors are passed to sh as script content rather than reliably failing as a download error (and empty successful downloads run as a no-op), weakening failure detection.

findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into shell at build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes mutable remote content as root during the build with no version pin, checksum, or signature verification, and the result is baked into the shipped image. Compromise of the host or any redirect target yields arbitrary code execution in the build and image. The same pipeline also masks download failure: the pipeline status is `sh`'s, so a failed `curl` feeding empty input to `sh` can exit 0 and produce an image silently missing whatever the script installs.

findings.title: Stop discarding ErrMissing in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for a missing key at src/store.go:7-12, but LoadOrDefault discards that error at line 16 and returns "". This is indistinguishable from a key that is present with an empty-string value, so any caller of this exported API can persist or report a missing-key failure as a legitimate empty value. The name also promises a default, yet the signature accepts no default value and always falls back to "".

findings.title: Restore completion guarantee before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every result had been received from the channel. Now it returns immediately after spawning goroutines, so a caller using the standard producer pattern of calling Run and then closing results can panic with 'send on closed channel', and a caller that proceeds after Run can lose results or exit before they are delivered.

findings.title: Preserve input order of emitted results
findings.whyItBreaks: The channel carries only doubled ints with no job identifier, so positional order is the only way a caller can correlate results with jobs. Sequential code emitted them in jobs order; concurrent goroutines race to send, making the output order nondeterministic and silently scrambling that correlation.

findings.title: Stop spawned senders blocking forever when consumption stops
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job spawns a goroutine that blocks indefinitely on 'results <- j * 2' with no select on ctx.Done(). If the receiver stops draining or the context is cancelled, len(jobs) detached goroutines leak permanently; Run has already returned so the caller cannot stop or reap them. The context parameter is accepted but never used.

findings.title: Wait for spawned goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run launches one goroutine per job and returns immediately, whereas previously it returned only after every send on results had completed. A caller using the previous guarantee can now close(results) after Run returns and cause a goroutine to panic with 'send on closed channel', or check/exit after Run returns and silently lose results that have not been sent yet. The signature provides no WaitGroup, done channel, or other completion signal to replace the lost guarantee, and the detached goroutines also block forever on results if the receiver stops reading (they do not select on ctx.Done()).

findings.title: Restore Run completion guarantee before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run returns immediately after spawning goroutines, so a caller using the previous safe pattern Run(...); close(results) can panic with 'send on closed channel', and other callers have no point at which all results are known to be sent. If the receiver stops or ctx is cancelled, the spawned goroutines also block forever on results <- because the send does not select on ctx.Done(), leaking one goroutine per undelivered job.

findings.title: Preserve input order of results
findings.whyItBreaks: The original code sent j*2 values in jobs order, but the new goroutines race to send, so the sequence received from results is nondeterministically permuted. Any consumer that pairs results positionally with jobs, or otherwise relies on the established ordered delivery of this exported function, silently gets misassociated values.

findings.title: Use or remove the ignored tag parameter in Log

A caller such as Log("failed", "auth") receives log output with no "auth" tag, indistinguishable from an untagged message, so the logged data a caller/log consumer receives is missing the supplied tag. Previously token_hash(...) == stored_hash evaluated to False for those values, so guard() returned 401. Now the TypeError propagates unhandled through guard() at app/token.py:14, turning a missing/corrupt/bytes-valued stored hash (e.g. absent DB record) into a 500/crash instead of a 401 rejection.

findings.title: Handle missing or non-ASCII stored hashes without raising TypeError

If stored_hash is None, bytes, or a non-ASCII string—for example when no stored token exists or stored data is malformed—the previous == comparison returned False and guard() returned 401, whereas compare_digest raises TypeError and guard() fails with an exception instead of denying access cleanly.

findings.title: Restore timeoutMs or add a backward-compatible alias
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported Config renames timeoutMs to timeout and adds required retries. findings.title: Propagate final failure from retryBackground instead of silent void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground catches every error thrown by fn, and when attempts are exhausted or the deadline passes it implicitly returns void, exactly as it does after a successful call. This exported public path forces every caller to conflate total failure with success, so a background operation can be lost with no error signal to log, retry upstream, or report.

findings.title: Restore timeoutMs or keep it as a compatible alias
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported, so renaming required timeoutMs to timeout breaks existing TypeScript consumers at compile time. An unmigrated JavaScript caller passing {maxAttempts, timeoutMs} gets config.timeout === undefined, deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN at src/retry.ts:8, and the guard Date.now() > deadline at src/retry.ts:10 is always false for NaN, so the timeout is silently never enforced.

findings.title: Remove duplicate retryBackground and synonymous retries field

findings.title: Do not make retryBackground failure indistinguishable from success
findings.whyItBreaks: The added public function discards every thrown error in the empty catch at lines 27-28, then falls off the end at line 31 (or returns on timeout at line 23) with the same void result as the success return at lines 25-26. A caller cannot distinguish success from exhausted retries or timeout and may proceed as if fn succeeded. Per Trigger D this exported swallow site is defective even with no in-repo caller yet.

Untyped or persisted old configs instead get config.timeout === undefined, so deadline becomes NaN at src/retry.ts:8; substituting that value into the guard at src/retry.ts:10 gives Date.now() > NaN === false on every iteration, so the timeout silently never fires.

findings.title: Do not swallow all retryBackground failures as void success
findings.whyItBreaks: The added public function discards every error from fn in the empty catch and returns void identically for success, deadline expiry, exhausted attempts, and retries <= 0 never invoking fn, so no caller can distinguish failure from success or avoid acting on work that never ran. findings.title: Render the field value instead of its length label

For a number such as 42, length is undefined at runtime (rendering len=undefined), and under TypeScript this is TS2339 because length does not exist on number, so the widened contract is not implemented and can break compilation.

findings.whyItBreaks: Previously <input defaultValue={value} /> displayed the caller's value; now it displays len=<length>. findings.title: Remove step that echoes deployment secret to workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The step expands secrets.TOKEN into the step environment and prints it with echo, sending the credential value to workflow log output. GitHub's automatic masking is best-effort and must not be relied on for a deliberately printed secret (e.g. short, multiline, or transformed values can evade masking), and anyone able to view or export the logs/artifacts becomes part of the secret's exposure surface. The step also does not make TOKEN available to the subsequent `make build` step, because env is scoped to this step only, so it exposes the secret without enabling the deploy build.

findings.title: Remove step that prints deployment token to workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The step injects secrets.TOKEN into a shell whose only action is `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, exposing the credential to retained workflow logs and relying solely on GitHub's best-effort log masking. The token has no legitimate consumer here: the following `make build` step does not receive TOKEN, so the added exposure provides no deploy functionality.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects secrets.TOKEN into the shell only to print it with echo. This unnecessarily exposes the credential to workflow log handling and relies solely on runner masking; masking does not cover transformed/split values and GitHub explicitly warns against passing secrets to the shell for printing. Anyone with access to retained run logs becomes part of the exposure surface, and the step provides no build or deploy function.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now uses Node spawnSync's default 1MiB maxBuffer. It is called at line 140 for `git diff mergeBase headSha`, so any PR patch over ~1MiB is killed with a maxBuffer error; res.status !== 0 then throws `git diff ... failed:` (with empty/misleading stderr) and the whole review fails. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers at lines 19 and 29 retain 64MiB, showing large-output handling is required here.

findings.title: Report mergeBase as bundle baseSha to match patch
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141) are computed against mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) at line 139, but the bundle now labels baseSha as that base. When PR_BASE_SHA (line 138, the base-branch tip) has advanced past the branch point, baseSha != mergeBase, so the bundle's baseSha/headSha pair describes a different diff than bundle.patch: any downstream inspection of `git diff baseSha..headSha` re-introduces unrelated base-branch changes (inverted) that are not in the patch, mis-scoping the review. In the fallback path baseSha already equals the merge-base, so only the Actions/PR_BASE_SHA path regresses.

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer on git() so large PR diffs do not fail
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer drops spawnSync to Node's 1 MiB default. git() at line 140 runs `git diff mergeBase headSha`, whose output routinely exceeds 1 MiB on large PRs (lockfiles, generated code, vendored changes); spawnSync then kills the process with ENOBUFS, res.status is null, and line 38 throws a bare `git diff ... failed:` error, aborting the whole review. The sibling gh/ghText helpers at lines 19 and 29 retain the 64 MiB buffer, showing the limit was deliberate for exactly this kind of payload.

findings.title: Keep Bundle.baseSha as mergeBase to match patch and changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141) are computed from mergeBase, but the bundle now labels them with baseSha. When PR_BASE_SHA is set and the base branch has advanced past the fork point, baseSha != mergeBase, so the bundle is internally inconsistent: `git diff bundle.baseSha bundle.headSha` does not equal bundle.patch and includes reverse changes from base-branch commits that are not part of the PR. Any downstream consumer that re-derives the diff, checks out base files, or validates findings against baseSha will review phantom changes and misattribute them to the PR. Previously baseSha: mergeBase kept the triple (baseSha, headSha, patch) consistent by construction.

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer for git subprocesses
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores Node spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The git() call at line 140 returns the full PR patch (git diff mergeBase..headSha); any patch over 1 MiB triggers a maxBuffer error, git()'s status check at lines 38-40 throws (with an empty stderr message, since git itself succeeded), and runGithub's catch posts a failing check and exits 1 — so the review fails entirely on large PRs. The sibling gh/ghText helpers at lines 19 and 29 retain 64 MiB, confirming the intended limit.

findings.title: Report mergeBase, not baseSha, in the review bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changedFiles are computed from mergeBase (lines 140-141), but the bundle now labels baseSha (line 165) as the base. When PR_BASE_SHA is the base branch tip and that branch has advanced since the PR branched, baseSha != mergeBase (line 139). The review() consumer at line 177 then receives an inconsistent pair: any recomputation such as git diff baseSha..headSha or git show baseSha:<file> includes or reverses intervening base-branch changes that are not in the supplied patch/changedFiles, producing wrong file contents or spurious findings. The bug is hidden only when the base branch has not moved.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for Codex review subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex passes a prompt containing untrusted reviewed code/diff as stdin to `codex exec` with cwd set to the reviewed repo at lines 23-26. The removed `-s read-only` was the only sandbox enforcement in this call; without it the sandbox falls back to Codex's default and the user's ambient Codex configuration, which may be workspace-write or danger-full-access. A prompt-injected instruction in the reviewed diff could then modify or delete files in the checkout being reviewed, or outside it under danger-full-access, instead of only returning review text.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for spawned Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously '-s read-only' guaranteed the spawned agent could not write regardless of environment. With the flag omitted, Codex falls back to $CODEX_HOME/config.toml (sandbox_mode/default_permissions), so a common workspace-write setting lets model-generated commands modify or delete files in opts.repoPath (spawn cwd at line 24, prompt fed via stdin at line 25), and danger-full-access gives unrestricted filesystem/network access. That silently converts a read-only reviewer over potentially untrusted PR content into a writer and lets it tamper with the tree under review; behavior now varies by machine.

findings.title: Restore pinned read-only sandbox for Codex execution
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `-s read-only`, so `codex exec` no longer pins its sandbox policy. Per `codex exec --help`, `-s/--sandbox` selects the policy for model-generated shell commands (`read-only|workspace-write|danger-full-access`) and `-c` describes values otherwise loaded from `~/.codex/config.toml`; omitting `-s` therefore inherits the user's configured/default policy instead of guaranteeing read-only. `runCodex` feeds a prompt (in this review-agent context, containing untrusted PR diff content) to Codex with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, so under a common `workspace-write` config — or `danger-full-access` — prompt-injected or mistaken model commands can modify the repository under review (or the wider filesystem), tainting the review and risking data loss. The function only needs the text returned via `--output-last-message`, which the CLI writes itself, so write access is not required.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before diffing PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and that branch has advanced after the PR branch diverged, baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD. `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot tree diff, so commits present only on the base appear as reversed changes/deletions in patch, and changedFileSet likewise lists base-only files as PR-changed. Those enter Bundle.patch/changedFiles at src/adapters/github.ts:162-172 and changedPaths filtering at src/adapters/github.ts:61-63, so the review can flag, comment on, or request changes for code the PR never touched. The fallback path masks this only because it already returns a merge-base at src/adapters/github.ts:138.

findings.title: Use merge-base instead of raw base SHA for PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the base branch tip and main has advanced since the PR forked (baseSha not an ancestor of headSha/HEAD), git diff baseSha HEAD is a two-dot diff: it includes the reversal of every main-only commit since the fork point, not just the PR's changes. Those main-only files enter patch and changedFiles/changedPaths, so the reviewer reviews and can comment on/request changes for code the PR never touched, and files changed on both branches are misrepresented. The deleted merge-base(baseSha, headSha) computation existed exactly to reduce baseSha to the fork point in this case; in the fallback path baseSha is already a merge-base, so the old call was only load-bearing when PR_BASE_SHA names a diverged base tip.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so base-branch changes are not reviewed as PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and that branch advanced after the PR diverged, git diff baseSha HEAD is a two-dot diff: it includes the reverse of base-side commits as well as the PR changes. The reviewer therefore receives files and hunks the PR never touched, changedFiles/changedPaths are inflated, and inline findings can be emitted for non-PR files/lines (GitHub then rejects or misplaces them, and postReview's fallback silently drops inline comments). The old merge-base(baseSha, headSha) diff was the three-dot equivalent and was also correct when baseSha was already the merge-base fallback on line 138. The switch from headSha to literal HEAD additionally decouples the patch from bundle.headSha/postReview commit_id when PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checkout.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid $-pattern substitution in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement specially: '$$' collapses to '$', '$&' becomes the matched placeholder, '$`' inserts the prompt text before the placeholder, and "$'" inserts the prompt text after it; a function replacement is inserted literally, as the base code did. bundle JSON, candidate JSON, and especially the raw arbitrary PR-controlled bundle.patch on line 33 can contain these sequences (e.g. reviewed code using replace(), shell, or Makefiles). Such a patch is therefore mangled or causes large prompt sections to be duplicated in the text sent to runCodex, so the reviewer/critic can miss or misjudge findings based on corrupted patch/findings content.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid $-pattern substitution in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement specially: '$$' becomes '$', '$&' becomes the matched placeholder (e.g. '{{PATCH}}'), '$`' inserts the prompt prefix and "$'" inserts the entire prompt suffix. bundle.patch and the JSON-stringified bundle/candidate are arbitrary reviewed code/diffs that routinely contain '$$', '$&', '$`' or "$'" (shell, Make, JS replace, regex); such a patch is silently mangled or embeds duplicated prompt text in reviewPrompt/criticPrompt sent to runCodex at lines 28/34, so the model reviews corrupted data and can miss or invent findings. The previous '() => ...' replacers inserted the value literally.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid $-pattern corruption
findings.whyItBreaks: With a string replacement, String.prototype.replace interprets $$ as $, $& as the matched placeholder, $` as the prompt text before the placeholder, and $' as the prompt text after it. bundle JSON embeds the arbitrary patch and agentsMd, candidate JSON contains arbitrary finding text, and bundle.patch is an arbitrary diff; any of them containing e.g. "$&" (common in replace/shell code under review) is rewritten to "{{BUNDLE}}"/"{{FINDINGS}}"/"{{PATCH}}", "$$" is collapsed to "$", and $`/$' duplicate chunks of the prompt into the injected content. The reviewer and critic therefore analyze mangled code/findings instead of the verbatim input, which can hide or invent defects. The previous () => ... replacers returned the text literally and were load-bearing.

findings.title: Pin fallback review to the reviewed head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha is captured before the review is computed (lines 141-144, 183), and the primary path pins the GitHub review to it via commit_id at line 89. The fallback now omits commit_id, and GitHub defaults it to the PR's most recent commit. If a commit is pushed during the review and the primary POST then fails (e.g. an inline comment is rejected), the fallback posts the old diff's COMMENT/REQUEST_CHANGES verdict against the unreviewed new head, where it can block or mislabel that code instead of the reviewed commit.

findings.title: Fallback review loses commit pin and can attach to unreviewed head
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary review payload pins commit_id to headSha (src/adapters/github.ts:88-89), and headSha is captured before the awaited review runs (src/adapters/github.ts:141,181-183), so the PR head can advance during review. The fallback POST now omits commit_id, so GitHub defaults the review to the PR's current head: a REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT verdict computed from the old diff can be recorded against newer, unreviewed commits (and, if the primary failed because the reviewed SHA was force-pushed away, the fallback silently re-targets the replacement head instead of failing).

findings.title: Fallback review loses commit pin and can attach to unreviewed head
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary review pins commit_id=headSha (lines 88-93), but the fallback no longer sends commit_id. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the most recent commit in the PR. headSha is captured at line 141 before the potentially long review() call at line 181; if a new commit is pushed in that window and the primary POST then fails (e.g. an invalid inline comment), the fallback posts the REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT body computed for headSha against the newer, unreviewed commit, so GitHub does not mark it outdated for the commit it actually reviewed.

findings.title: Do not fabricate P1 findings from invalid severity or category
findings.whyItBreaks: An invalid or missing severity now becomes P1 and an invalid category becomes bug instead of throwing in strict mode or being dropped when strict=false. Malformed model output is therefore indistinguishable from a real, potentially blocking P1 finding.

findings.title: Do not emit findings with empty file or invalid line numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing file, title, whyItBreaks, and suggestedFix now become empty strings, while missing lines become 0 and non-numeric lines become NaN via Number(...). Previously these malformed findings threw; now unanchorable Finding objects pass normalization, and NaN serializes to null despite the numeric type.

findings.title: Restore the removed strict parameter on normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported, so removing its second parameter breaks TypeScript callers that pass strict and silently reverses JavaScript callers passing strict=false: malformed entries that were dropped are now retained after defaulting, and a null entry crashes at line 96 with a TypeError instead of being dropped.

findings.title: Stop fabricating P1 findings from malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeFinding threw on invalid severity/category and missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix/invalid line numbers, and normalizeReview in strict mode propagated that error. Now an input such as {} or {severity:"P9"} becomes {severity:"P1", category:"bug", file:"", lineStart:0, lineEnd:0, whyItBreaks:"", suggestedFix:""}: a failure signal is downgraded to a plausible-looking P1 finding that downstream reporting cannot distinguish from a real finding. This is an exported/public swallow site, so the defective API contract ships even with no in-repo caller. Non-numeric lineStart additionally yields NaN instead of the previous finite/positive rejection.

findings.title: Restore normalizeReview strict parameter and its drop-on-malformed mode
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature changes from normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) to normalizeReview(raw). TypeScript callers passing a second argument now fail compilation, and JavaScript callers passing strict=false silently lose the documented behavior of dropping malformed findings via try/catch/filter; instead line 131 maps every entry through the new lenient normalizeFinding and keeps fabricated findings. Both existing modes of a public API are broken by one signature change.

findings.title: Restore validation instead of fabricating P1 findings from malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting {} now yields severity P1, category bug, empty file, lineStart 0, lineEnd 0, and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix instead of the previous 'malformed finding' error; a non-numeric lineStart yields NaN. Malformed model output is therefore indistinguishable from a genuine high-severity finding and can drive the verdict and location rendering with no anchor or rationale.

findings.title: Restore normalizeReview strict flag and lenient filtering of bad findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the second parameter is a breaking change to this exported function: TypeScript callers passing strict=false no longer compile, and JavaScript callers silently lose lenient mode. A findings array containing null now aborts the whole review with a TypeError when reading raw.severity at line 96 instead of filtering that entry as strict=false previously did.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch only runs for workflow_dispatch (pull_request events set EVENT_HEAD), and it is the first step, before Checkout PR head at lines 42-46, so no git checkout/remote exists in $GITHUB_WORKSPACE on a clean self-hosted runner. Without -R "$REPO" (and with no GH_REPO env), `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` cannot determine the base repository ('failed to determine base repo'), yielding empty head/base outputs; checkout and the review then run with empty refs. A stale workspace from a prior run may mask this, making manual dispatch flaky rather than reliably broken.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch runs only on workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD empty), and this step runs before actions/checkout (lines 42-46), so there is no local git repo/remotes for gh to infer the repository from and no GH_REPO is set. Verified: `gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid` in a non-git directory fails with 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository'; gh help environment documents GH_REPO/-R as the mechanism for commands that otherwise operate on a local repository. Manual dispatch therefore resolves empty/failing head/base SHAs instead of the requested PR's, breaking the documented manual-trigger path (pull_request events are unaffected via the EVENT_HEAD branch).

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in manual dispatch path
findings.whyItBreaks: These lines run only when EVENT_HEAD is empty (workflow_dispatch), and the Resolve PR refs step precedes Checkout PR head (line 42), so the workspace has no checked-out .git/remote on a clean runner. Without -R "$REPO" (or GH_REPO), gh cannot determine the repository: verified `gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid` in a non-git directory exits 1 with 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository'. Because the call is inside $(...) in an echo, the failure is masked and head=/base= are written empty, so checkout and the review run with empty PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA instead of the requested PR's refs. The pull_request path is unaffected, but the documented manual-trigger path (line 13) is broken on any fresh/cleaned self-hosted workspace and only accidentally works if a stale checkout's .git remains.

findings.title: Restore failure signal when review output is malformed
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw on non-object input and on missing/non-string summary or non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. The new code maps every such failure to String(raw?.summary ?? ""), [] findings, [] checked and [] residual_risks, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate clean review with zero findings. This exported normalizer therefore forces any caller to treat malformed/unparseable reviewer output as a successful empty review, silently dropping the error signal (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Restore malformed-review errors instead of returning empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeReview threw 'malformed review output' for a non-object input or missing/wrong-typed summary, findings, checked, or residual_risks. Now normalizeReview(null), {}, or output missing findings returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings. A caller therefore cannot distinguish model/parse failure from a clean review and can report or act on the empty result as a pass, silently dropping all findings and blocking risks.

findings.title: Restore throw on malformed review instead of returning empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeReview threw 'malformed review output' for a non-object input or a missing/non-string summary, non-array findings, non-array checked, or non-array residual_risks. Now null, {}, and other malformed inputs return {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate review that found nothing. findings.title: Restore GitHub token stripping before spawning Codex

findings.title: Restore GitHub token stripping before spawning Codex

That subprocess processes prompt content (in this review-agent context, untrusted PR diffs) with a model that can run read-only shell commands such as `env`; the read-only sandbox restricts writes, not reading the process environment or emitting values into --output-last-message, which runCodex returns to its caller. A prompt-injected or curious subprocess can therefore surface a live GitHub credential the parent holds for fetching/posting PRs, defeating the deliberate least-privilege scrub. findings.title: Restore fork guard on self-hosted review runner

Without it, any fork PR (opened/synchronize/reopened, lines 7-9) now runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18), checks out the attacker-controlled PR head SHA (lines 20-24), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against that checkout (lines 26-28), and then directly executes attacker-controlled code via `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) with `GH_TOKEN` in the environment (line 33) and a token granted `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` (lines 12-14).
